https://www.dw.com/en/colombia-earthquak.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IZRh The powerful 7.4 magnitude quake struck early on Monday morning, causing widespread damage in Manizales and other cities Image: Giovanny Galvez/AFP Advertisement A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning. Around six hours after the quake struck, Colombia's president said that 111 people had been confirmed dead around the country. Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities. The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast. What is the latest? Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency. He said that locating anyone still potentially trapped was the highest priority for rescuers and declared a national state of emergency. "As of 12:30 [local time], the toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, with 1,575 homes damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, and 18 health centers and 52 schools damaged," de la Espriella said from Bogota. Multiple deaths after major earthquake in Colombia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU stands "ready to provide more support" to Colombia. The bloc's satellite service, Copernicus, has already been mobilized to aid rescuers. "Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia," she wrote on social media. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia." What's happening on the ground? The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside. "Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin." Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, said that at least 27 people had died in the quake, in numbers issued prior to the president's address. Officials in Risaralda had said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor. The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were 12 dead and 84 wounded in her district as of lunch time local time. And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira. Residents in Cali tried to rush to safety in the aftermath of Monday's earthquake Image: Santiago Saldarriaga/AP Photo/picture alliance Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined. "Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list. What do we know about the quake's size and location? The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well. The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border. One of the towers at the Cathedral of Manizales was damaged by the quake Image: John Jairo Bonilla/AP Photo/picture alliance The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south. The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter. The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors . Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela. USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake. The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: ‘It starts here’: is the AfD’s win in Saxony-Anhalt just the beginning for the far-right’s European resurgence? Photograph: Matthias Schräder/AP View image in fullscreen ‘It starts here’: is the AfD’s win in Saxony-Anhalt just the beginning for the far-right’s European resurgence? Photograph: Matthias Schräder/AP First Edition newsletter The far right Tuesday briefing: What happens next after Germany’s far-right breakthrough? In today’s newsletter: The AfD’s local election triumph has shocked Europe, and raised questions about how to counter the rising far right Libby Brooks Tue 8 Sep 2026 01.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. Across Germany – and Europe more widely – there has been a palpable sense of shock and disbelief after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) swept to a historic state election victory in the early hours of Monday. It was, according to France’s European affairs minister, Benjamin Haddad, “a very grave moment for Europe”. The resonance was stark in the UK too: as the results came in, hundreds of black-clad activists intent on blocking migrant arrivals were battling with police for a second night along England’s south coast. While seasoned observers stress the context that Saxony-Anhalt, a small state in the former communist east of the country, has traditionally voted further to the right, a red line has been crossed. A far-right party has been propelled to the brink of power at regional level in Germany for the first time since the Nazis – despite 13 years of increasingly desperate efforts by mainstream parties to shut them out of government. For today’s newsletter, I spoke to the Guardian’s Berlin correspondent Kate Connolly from the state capital Magdeburg, and our Europe correspondent, Jon Henley, about why Germany’s famous firewall against the far right has failed, and what happens next. First, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories UK news | Batons and synthetic pepper spray were used to repel hundreds of masked, black-clad vigilantes in Portsmouth on Sunday, it has emerged , as the policing minister said officers had been injured as they repelled organised “aggression”. Israel | Ed Miliband will announce what he has described as a broad reset of the UK’s relations with Israel on Tuesday, promising the government will take a more active approach in supporting the Palestinian cause. US | The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”. Climate crisis | Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility. UK politics | There is little appetite for cuts to disability benefits even among Conservative and Reform voters, and proposals to reduce spending could prove politically risky, according to an authoritative national survey . In depth: ‘A palpable sense of disbelief’ View image in fullscreen Ulrich Siegmund, leader of the AfD party in Saxony-Anhalt, has been labelled Germany’s “most dangerous man” by Der Spiegel. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock The first person Kate spoke to when she arrived in Magdeburg on Monday afternoon was a paramedic named Eric, who was fundraising for a local hospice. He explained how his father had spent years working to obtain a German passport after migrating from Guinea. “Already that day he felt the mood on the street had become more hostile,” Kate told me. I know from experience how difficult it can be to persuade strangers to elaborate on their private voting decisions – especially when you have copy to file in a hurry – but yesterday was different, she said: “Everybody had very profound thoughts to share.” She described conversations with a “heartbroken” older couple, who had grown up under communism; a 16-year-old who arrived from Syria under Angela Merkel’s open borders policy in 2015 and was frightened she would be first on the list to send back; another woman who’d voted for the AfD and said she didn’t appreciate being “tarred with the same brush” as supporters of Hitler in the 1930s. Kate interviewed her as they stood by a Stolperstein, a memorial plaque to a victim of Nazi persecution. As we spoke, thousands were gathering at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate to express their opposition to the AfD, and where there was a palpable sense of disbelief and dread as news of the results filtered. Why is the AfD on the rise? The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, was elected leader of the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in 2022 on a pledge to halve the AfD’s vote. Instead it has doubled, and support for his centrist coalition that has tumbled. A “deeply shocked” Merz vowed to stay in office yesterday after the nativist party triumphed with 44% of the vote, just short of an absolute majority The turnout in Saxony-Anhalt was breathtaking. At 77.8%, compared with 60.3% in 2021, it suggests the AfD – classified as extremist by Germany’s security services – has succeeded in energising many who didn’t vote at all five years ago. Detailed polling analysis suggests that, while one in three AfD supporters align with the party’s extremist ideology, its growing popularity is driven by a diversity of voters who feel alienated from mainstream politics . Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, is a charismatic former perfume salesman who has weaponised voter discontent around the faltering economy and migration – even though irregular immigration has reduced since Merz came into office. Research from 2023 found a direct link between rent increases – particularly amonglower income voters – and likelihood of supporting the AfD. Last month, Der Spiegel put Siegmund on its front cover, with the tagline “Germany’s most dangerous man”. He responded by filming himself signing copies for his 800,000 TikTok followers. Siegmund has capitalised on a mood of ostalgie – nostalgia for communist East Germany – and bubbling resentment among poorer east Germans who view themselves as second-class citizens compared to people from the west. Strikingly, it appears one of the highest shares of the AfD’s vote came from the 35- to 44 age group, who were children or infants when the Berlin Wall came down. What does the result mean for Germany? There’s now debate about whether the previous consensus over how mainstream parties should deal with the far right – the so-called “Brandmauer”, or firewall – has horribly backfired. Sceptics believe this non-cooperation with AfD at any level from local councils up to federal government has allowed the party to escape the scrutiny that comes with holding office. Another criticism is that it has neutered the political mainstream. “The argument runs that in order to keep the far right out, it forces mainstream parties into unnatural coalitions,” Jon says. The compromises that they have to strike have resulted in ineffective government and in turn feeds the extremes further.” Now, there are complex coalition talks ahead for the parties in Saxony-Anhalt. While Siegmund has rejected leading a minority administration, initial indications are that the AfD could govern with the hard-left, pro-Russian Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht party, which received 5.3% of the vote. If he succeeds in becoming the state’s first far-right governor, Siegmund will have control over significant policy areas including education, policing and public broadcasting. AfD has already proposed revisions to the school curriculum, in what one party member described as “more Bismarck, less Hitler”, as well as defunding anti-racism initiatives and removing pride flags. Jon also suggests the AfD might make changes to civil service recruitment “to create a more supportive environment”. But securing the Saxony-Anhalt government would also give the AfD seats in the Bundesrat upper house: while they wouldn’t have enough seats to block legislation they could still act as a disruptive force. And with the AfD leading the polls nationally, there’s a likely ripple effect across the country. There are more state elections later this month – including in traditionally liberal Berlin, where the AfD is now polling at 18%, with the CDU maintaining a slim lead in the early 20s. If their vote share rises across states, options for coalition building without the AfD become increasingly convoluted, further flattening the mainstream’s ability to govern confidently. … And for Europe? Not all of Europe’s far-right leaders have welcomed this development. Jon, who is based in Paris, has been listening to France’s National Rally – which under Marine Le Pen has spent years successfully detoxifying its image – on the airwaves insisting that, in his words, “these guys are way too extreme for us”. To give you one example, two years ago the National Rally expelled the AfD from its European parliamentary group, which includes Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, following revelations that the party backed mass deportations and downplayed the crimes of the Nazi SS. But any domestic shock waves in Europe’s largest economy will inevitably affect the bloc. “A weakened German government in complete upheaval would obviously be bad news for Europe,” says Jon. “It could affect things like the bloc’s policy towards migration; the environment, because the AfD is famously climate-sceptic; and Ukraine, because it’s also pretty much pro-Kremlin.” In a press conference yesterday, an ashen-faced Merz drew a fairly explicit link between the AfD and Russia, noting that “2,500 km in the east, the election results were being celebrated.” This may reflect growing calls within the CDU and their coalition partner, the Social Democrats, for Merz to toughen his stance on Russia. After a drone attack on Leipzig airport in August, the German government took a month before publicly blaming Moscow , though the language could not have been more direct when foreign minister Johann Wadephul stated: “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.” With a series of federal or presidential elections taking place in Spain, France, Italy, Poland, and Germany over the next two years, the AfD’s landslide can be viewed as an indication of coming peril and a challenge on how to meet it. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion “The far right’s ideas have been steadily normalised by the media and the political centre,” says Jon. “They have completely framed the immigration debate, and everybody else is just scrambling to react to them”. As Keir Starmer’s government discovered with Reform in the UK, repurposing populist rhetoric doesn’t convince disaffected voters. “Political scientists across Europe would say this result is down to that, and the failure by mainstream parties to come up with inspiring policies that will actually make a real difference to people’s lives and address some of the reasons why they choose to vote for the far right,” he said. For more on the far right in Europe, sign up to This Is Europe , our free weekly with selection of the most pressing stories and debates . What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen ‘In fact, we’ll be blood brothers for life. Come on, buddy. Let’s go home,’ what Brian Clark said to Stanley Praimnath when he saved him on the 81st floor of the north tower. Photograph: Courtesy Brian Clark I thought David Smith’s re-telling of 9/11 , through the eyes of two strangers who met in the middle of the smoke and became some of the only people who survived the incident, was brilliant. Poppy Noor, newsletters team Nesrine Malik is the best voice in Britain writing about Israel and Gaza . Her column on the horrific plans of Israeli ministers is well worth your time. Hettie One of the most interesting things about working at the Guardian is the letters we get from our readers. This recent series of responses about how to solve the prisons crisis made many good suggestions. Hettie I enjoyed Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor’s recent piece in the Financial Times (£) about “end times fascism” and the Nazi warships revealed as rivers in eastern Europe dried up this summer. Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor will be speaking at a Guardian event later this month ( tickets here ). Hettie The Guardian Australia has just launched a new politics newsletter to bring you up to speed on the stories that really matter, and what they mean for you. Sign up here . Sport View image in fullscreen Zheng Qinwen waves to the crowd after booking her spot in the last eight at Flushing Meadows. Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPA US Open | Zheng Qinwen recovered from 5-0 down in the opening set to stun Iga Świątek and reach the last eight of the US Open, while Elena Rybakina beat Naomi Osaka 6-1 6-4. Cricket | Pakistan have launched an investigation into the “discipline and conduct” during their tour of England, with two players understood to have had their mobile phones confiscated as part of the probe. F1 | Bernie Ecclestone was detained in Portugal on Monday after customs authorities found him in possession of an undocumented shotgun. The front pages View image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian “UK hardens stance on Israel with ban on illegal settlements trade”, is the Guardian ’s front page today, while the Times has “PM to declare trade ban on settlements in West Bank”. The FT leads on “Pressure builds on Germany’s Merz as far-right AfD toasts ‘dream result’”, the i Paper says “New ISA to help Britain’s older first-time buyers”. On small boats protests Metro has “Port in a storm”, the Mirror says “Now they try to stop the lifeboats”, while the Express ’s take is “Don’t ignore public anger over illegal migrants”. The Telegraph splash with “King tells Harry: No return to the firm”, Mail writes “King puts Harry and Meghan in their place”, and the Sun writes “Megxit means Megxit”. Today in Focus: The Latest Photograph: The Guardian Far-right protesters descend on Dover and Portsmouth The government has condemned the ‘thuggish and intimating behaviour’ of far-right activists clad in black and balaclavas who caused disruption and unrest in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend in an attempt to obstruct asylum seekers arriving on small boats. The action was seemingly organised by Daniel Thomas, an agitator better known as Danny Tommo, who has close ties with the far-right extremist Tommy Robinson. Thomas was recorded on the ground saying Portsmouth was now ‘ground zero’ for small boat crossings, and has threatened further action. Lucy Hough speaks to political correspondent Ben Quinn. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings View image in fullscreen Illustration: Ben Jennings/The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen The much-celebrated beetles and their ‘love torches’ have vanished from the British countryside. Photograph: blickwinkel/Alamy For the first time in a century, glow-worms are shining again in North Yorkshire. In recent decades, the bioluminescent female invertebrates had vanished from the British countryside. But after a budget reintroduction programme led by volunteer “glow-getters”, they’ve been spotted over multiple weeks this summer at Nosterfield nature reserve near Ripon. https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/se.text: Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham at this year’s Venice film festival where they won the special jury prize for their documentary NAZA. Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham at this year’s Venice film festival where they won the special jury prize for their documentary NAZA. Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty Images Movies ‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directors Backing comes after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor were threatened with having their citizenship revoked and accused of treason Catherine Shoard in London and Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.44 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 14.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Film industry heavyweights across the globe have expressed solidarity with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the Oscar-winning Israeli directors of documentary NAZA, who have been threatened with having their citizenship revoked by Israel’s culture minister, who accused them of “treason against the state”. NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, is named for an acronym euphemistically used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza. It includes interviews with 24 Israeli military or intelligence soldiers and officers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza, resulting in the mass killing of Palestinian civilians. The film builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. The 80-minute documentary won the special jury prize at this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receiving a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. On Sunday, Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, accused the directors of being willing to “harm their homeland in order to receive applause from antisemites around the world”. View image in fullscreen Jonathan Glazer, Rachel Szor, Yuval Abraham and James Wilson in Venice. Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty Images “I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar wrote on X. Representatives for Venice, or the jury headed by Maggie Gyllenhaal, have not yet commented on these threats, but the artistic director of the Telluride film festival – widely acknowledged as the foremost Oscars launchpad – was swift to voice her outrage. “Documentary film-makers are among the best long-form journalists working and critical to our understanding of the world,” said Julie Huntsinger. “To even threaten their citizenship standing is unacceptable. This should be condemned by any thinking human.” Her words were echoed by the heads of the Locarno film festival, who said they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ right to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal. Artistic and journalistic freedom are the very foundation of what cinema can be: a space for dialogue which engages critically with the world we live in.” They added that they “reaffirm our support for film-makers who ask difficult questions and help us reflect”. NAZA will screen at the San Sebastián film festival next week. In a statement, its festival directors said the film “exposes the systematic genocide of the Palestinian people by the Israeli government” and that they stand “in solidarity” with the film’s makers as well as “the Palestinian people”. The documentary will show at the Bologna film festival tonight , before its North American premiere, at the New York film festival, later this month. ‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligence Read more Tricia Tuttle, director of the Berlin film festival, said: “Artists must be free to critically examine the world. Films can provoke discussion, disagreement and criticism, but in a democratic society, the response to art must be dialogue and scrutiny, not intimidation or punishment by the state. Our team at the Berlinale stands with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and all artists who exercise these rights.” Abraham and Szor won the documentary Oscar in 2025 for No Other Land, about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank, alongside their Palestinian co-directors Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. That film premiered at Berlin the previous year, where it won a prize. Following this victory, Abraham’s family home was targeted by a rightwing mob. “For me, that was the worst moment of all,” he told the Guardian last week. “My mum is hoping it doesn’t happen again.” Earlier this year, Tuttle’s position came under threat after several prize winners condemned Israel’s actions against Palestinians from the stage at the closing night awards gala. In the wake of this, the German culture minister, Wolfram Weimer, convened a crisis meeting as the Bild tabloid reported Tuttle was to be fired over giving “hate speech” an airing. In response, hundreds of prominent film-makers worldwide, including from Israel , rallied around Tuttle. View image in fullscreen Laura Poitras in Venice last week. Photograph: Alessandra Benedetti/Corbis/Getty Images In Israel, more than 1,500 film-makers have signed a petition in support of the directors, and refuting the accusation that they have sought to damage the country’s image internationally. Signatories include film-makers Liran Atzmor, one of the petition’s initiators, Nadav Lapid, Orna Ben Dor, Netalie Braun, Rani Blair, Hagai Levi, Shai Carmeli-Pollak and Shlomi Elkabetz. The petition calls on those who support freedom of expression and artistic freedom to stand in solidarity with Abraham and Szor. “In recent days, we have witnessed an unprecedented campaign of vilification and incitement against the film’s creators,” it says, warning that the rhetoric was moving increasingly close to “effectively sanctioning violence” and posed a physical threat to their lives. So far the Academy of Motion Pictures and Sciences has not commented on the situation in which its recent winners find themselves. However, previous recipients of the documentary award have done so. Laura Poitras, who won the documentary Oscar in 2015 for Citizenfour, about the WikiLeaks whistleblower Edward Snowden, defended the film’s factual credentials. “The facts about the mass killing of civilians in NAZA have been reported by the Guardian in dozens of rigorously fact-checked articles, and every assertion in the film is based on multiple sources,” said Poitras, who acted as a consultant on NAZA. View image in fullscreen No Other Land co-director Hamdan Ballal with his Oscar in March 2025, shortly after he had been attacked by Israeli settlers at his home, in his village of Susya in the occupied West Bank. Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP/Getty Images She called the threats by Israeli government officials “a threat to journalists worldwide. They are also familiar – my reporting with the Guardian on the National Security Authority’s illegal global mass surveillance was met with similar denials and attacks by the US government. “Despite the alarming nature of these current threats, it is important to emphasise that Israel has killed over 200 Palestinian journalists in Gaza and has normalised the murder of journalists.” Meanwhile Nan Goldin, the US photographer and activist who worked with Poitras on the 2022 Oscar-nominated documentary All the Beauty and Bloodshed, said she applauded NAZA’s directors “for their enormous courage in presenting a film that shows irrefutable proof of Israel’s war crimes at their own great risk.” British film industry veterans offering their support include director Richard Eyre , who said he was “beyond shocked by anything that the Israeli government does”, and the novelist and screenwriter Hanif Kureishi, who called the pair “both brave and admirable, standing up to state oppression, steadfast in their pursuit of the truth”. Israeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population. Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians. http://www.theuknews.com/news/279288864/.text: Israels shameful evasion of justice for Zomi Frankcom Independent Australia 04 Sep 2026, 07:30 GMT+10 Israels refusal to pursue criminal accountability for the killing of Zomi Frankcom and six fellow aid workers exposes a disturbing culture of impunity, writes DrBinoy Kampmark. IN SEPTEMBER 2025, nine countries launched theDeclaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel. Australia explained its important, if dark, inspiration in pursuing it: the slaying ofZomi Frankcom, along with six of her colleagues from the World Central Kitchen(WCK) charity, on 1 April 2024, by Israeli forces in Gaza. All perished in anattackconsisting of three missiles fired from a Hermes 450 drone in a stated deconflicted zone, despite clear logo markings on the convoy vehicles and extensivecoordinationregarding their movements with the Israeli authorities. The declaration, while lacking teeth, is at least a concession that individuals dedicated to protecting and preserving the vulnerable in conflict deserve a heftier shield of protection in international humanitarian law. It is all the more important given the systematic, weasel-worded libelling that the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) have pursued against the WCK workers. The murder of an Australian humanitarian worker in Gaza has again highlighted the deplorable hypocrisy of our Defence Department's ties to Israel, Binoy Kampmark writes. Behind the cover of bureaucratic plausibility and spreadsheet analysis, the Israeli authorities have conveniently packaged the charity worker with combat or terrorist groups, giving them equal standing in targeting. The disgraceful nature of this is evident in the refusal to consider any legal action for the events of that April. On 19 August, the IDFannouncedthat it had found no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation or the taking of additional measures against any of those involved in the incident. The spokespersons remarks initially gave ballast to the worthiness of the General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM), charged with making factual assessments of exceptional operational incidents, while using a range of tools and methodologies. It became very clear that these methodologies were heavily slanted toward conflating combatants and humanitarian workers on mere inferences. Consider, for instance, the IDFs alleged identification of a gunman on a truck in the humanitarian aid convoy while it was on a route to a warehouse for the unloading of the aid. The troops had identified vehicles surrounding the trucks in a manner that, in their assessment, and based on accumulated operational experience, corresponded to a scenario in which the Hamas terrorist organisation had taken control of the convoy. Despite serious failures in the process that led to the assessment that Hamas operatives were travelling in the vehicles, the decision to strike the convoy raised no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct. There had been, in the circumstances, a sufficient number of suspicious indicators. Much is done to shift the blame to the humanitarian workers. They had, for instance, hired an armed security force to accompany the convoy until the completion of the operation in order to protect it from seizure by armed actors in Gaza. This was not coordinated with the IDF authorities. The IDF had also attempted to contact WCK representatives in order to verify their assessment that the people in the vehicles were indeed not members of WCK. In an open letter to the Labor Government, Col Jennings implores condemnation of Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu for the murder of aid workers in Gaza. These efforts, so it is claimed, were made during the half-hour period that the vehicles were being tracked. (The assumption had already been made that they were Hamas operatives or workers in league with them.) The somewhat sickening insinuation here is that these humanitarians brought it upon themselves. Much the same view was expressed by the chief commander who ordered the strike, ColonelNochi Mendel. He has faced no legal proceedings, merely administrative action in the form of dismissal from his role as chief of staff of theNahalinfantry brigade. Mendel had been remiss in the IDFs rules of engagement and standard operating procedures. In an interview with theABCconducted in October 2025, Mendel had not favoured killing the WCK employees but was not sorry for what happened. Echoing the eventual findings of the investigation, the Colonel blamed an intermingling between the WCK and Hamas operatives that took place in an environment of evolving complexity. The suggestiveness and the euphemisms are all standard: that WCK had also made mistakes; that it was not really a neutral organisation. Not really an organisation you can say is innocent and completely clean. This lack of political sanitation was evidenced by ties to Hamas. The apologia is accordingly built up and inflated: operational fuzziness, the expediency that a conflict situation demands. No mention of the protocols governing such humanitarian convoys seemed to warrant discussion. Instead, Mendel could see, in a video feed, armed terrorists getting out and firing from the trucks. After the convoy arrived at a warehouse at Deir al Balah to unload the aid, We see them all mixed together both the WCK guys and the Hamas terrorists with weapons. Mendel cites a claim to being noble: that he could have ordered the attack there and then but preferred to wait so as not to harm the WCK. That turned out to be a cautionary note with little effect. Mendel then claims that the IDF did contact the WCK but not those in the convoy. A WCK representative from Europe was reached. The answer came: there arent supposed to be armed guards. The WCK personnel, after leaving the warehouse, then deviated from a coordinated prearranged route so says Mendel. This assessment by Dr Lee Duffield studies the decades-old origins of the fighting in Gaza and the moral dilemmas it has generated. This aided the decision to strike, but aninvestigation into the eventsby Australian Air Chief MarshalMark Binskinsuggests that the decision had already been reached by that point. It came as no surprise that WCK, in astatementon Mendels ruminations, regarded them as slanderous and lacking credibility. The decision not to initiate criminal proceedings, or to conduct a truly independent inquiry, baffled the governments whose nationals had died in the attack. The Israeli ambassadors of several countries were called in to give answers. Ajoint statementby the foreign ministries of Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom called the decision to close the case shameful. The Polish Foreign Minister,Radosaw Sikorski, was almost livid. Partnership requires respect, hestated. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for IDFs excessive use of force are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations. The goal of these operations, irrespective of the deaths they cause, is ultimately captured in chilling words by Mendel. There was no room to feel remorse here. The situation was very complex. Besides, the IDF had gone into Gaza to win, to eradicate this evil from the whole world, not just for ourselves. They were doing it for us. How easily does the righteous rhetoric of civilisation justify the unspeakable? DrBinoy Kampmarkwas a Cambridge Scholar and is a lecturer atRMIT University. You can follow Dr Kampmark@BKampmark. https://artsound.fm/events/an-evening-fo.text: Search in the website: Home / News / Events / An Evening for Nepal Live Music, Good Company, and a Cause Worth Showing Up For There’s something special about turning out for a good cause in person. Not just donating from behind a screen, but actually being there: sharing a room, a drink, and a few songs with fellow Canberrans who care about the same thing you do. That’s exactly what’s on offer on Sunday 20 September , when ArtSound FM joins forces with NKSSP Canberra (the Nepali Art, Culture and Literature Academy) for a warm, welcoming evening at the Polish White Eagle Club in Turner, all in support of families in Nepal whose lives have been upended by catastrophic flooding. You may have already heard the news: in late August, flash flooding and landslides tore through communities along the Nepal-China border, destroying homes, roads and livelihoods in a matter of hours. It’s the kind of disaster that’s easy to read about and hard to picture; until you think about it as neighbours losing everything overnight, with children and elderly residents among the most vulnerable. This is where a bit of Canberra community spirit can genuinely help. The Emergency Action Alliance brings together some of Australia’s most trusted aid organisations to get help where it’s needed most, quickly and efficiently. And every single dollar raised on the night — 100% of event profits — goes straight to their Nepal Flood Disaster Appeal. A relaxed Sunday evening, done properly This isn’t a solemn affair. Quite the opposite. Think of it as a proper community get-together: good music, a well-stocked bar, and the chance to catch up with familiar faces while doing something worthwhile. Two excellent local acts will be keeping the night lively: The Devil and The Bunny and The Daisy Coolective , both known for bringing warmth and energy to a room. The bar will be open all evening, with bar snacks on hand to keep you going. Whether you come for the music, the cause, or simply a pleasant Sunday evening out, you’ll leave knowing your ticket made a genuine difference to families who need it. The details When: Sunday 20 September 2026, 6:00pm–8:00pm (doors open 5:30pm) Where: Polish White Eagle Club (The Polo), 38 David Street, Turner ACT 2612 Tickets: $25 per adult, children under 12 free Music: The Devil and The Bunny + The Daisy Coolective Refreshments: Full bar service, with snacks available Where the money goes: 100% of profits donated directly to the Emergency Action Alliance Nepal Flood Disaster Appeal Make a Difference – Buy a Ticket Can’t make it on the night? You can still be part of this effort. Donations can be made directly to the appeal at any time: Online: emergencyaction.org.au/nepal-flood-appeal By phone: 1300 939 000 Every contribution, large or small, helps provide emergency shelter, clean water and medical care to families rebuilding their lives. We hope to see you there on the 20th — bring a friend, bring your appetite for good music, and let’s show Nepal that Canberra is standing with them. https://sana.sy/en/health/2346326/.text: Syrian Chargé d’Affaires Anas al-Badawi (R) meets Romanian Senator Titus Corlățean (L) in Bucharest, Romania, Sept. 27, 2026. Photo: SANA. Bucharest, Sept. 27 (SANA) Syria and Romania discussed reviving parliamentary links, while Syrian doctors living in Romania proposed forming an association to coordinate medical initiatives supporting Syria’s healthcare sector, the Syrian Embassy in Bucharest and participants said. Parliamentary ties Syrian Chargé d’Affaires Anas al-Badawi met Romanian Senator Titus Corlățean , chairman of the Senate’s Foreign Affairs Committee, to discuss restoring bilateral ties and strengthening political and parliamentary contacts, the embassy said in a post on X. The talks covered reactivating parliamentary friendship committees, exchanging expertise and expanding cooperation between Syria’s People’s Assembly and the Romanian Parliament. The Romanian side expressed interest in developing relations with Syria, and both sides agreed to work toward a joint plan for cooperation in areas of mutual interest, according to the embassy. Medical association proposed In a separate meeting hosted by the embassy, al-Badawi and Syrian medical professionals living in Romania discussed cooperation with health institutions in both countries and ways to use the doctors’ experience to support healthcare in Syria. Al-Badawi told SANA the embassy was ready to help address difficulties facing Syrian doctors in Romania and support initiatives that connect them with medical institutions in Syria. Participants discussed exchanging expertise, medical consultations, training and voluntary missions to treat patients in Syria. Dr. Mahmoud Orfali, an organizer of the proposed association, said it would help Syrian doctors in Romania coordinate and develop joint initiatives with institutions in both countries. He said volunteer delegations could provide treatment and perform surgeries in Syria. Hematology and oncology specialist Dr. Lin al-Akka said doctors were willing to join the association’s founding meeting and use their skills to serve patients in Syria. General surgeon Dr. Abdullah Qaddour said it could also help provide consultations and train healthcare workers. Participants agreed to continue coordinating across Romanian cities and develop plans for an association representing different medical specialties. kA/MF Jordan Reaffirms Support for the Stability of Syria and Lebanon Lebanon’s army chief says relations with Syria are good , coordination continues Geneva mine action conference focuses on war remnants, recovery efforts in Syria Acting Minister of Health discusses healthcare cooperation with Shammout Group Idlib governor meets with local dignitaries to discuss community, service issues press Photos Video Miscellaneous TAGGED: Anas al-Badawi healthcare People’s Assembly Romania Syria Share This Article Facebook Whatsapp Whatsapp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Editors Choice 20 people injured in traffic accidents and fires across Syria in past 24 hours October 11, 2026 Syria, Meta discuss restoring commercial services on social media platforms October 11, 2026 Arab, Islamic condemnations mount over Houthi attack on Riyadh airport October 11, 2026 Syria’s al-Qatir Cave in Raqqa remains largely unexplored October 11, 2026 Sign in to your account
